opus-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to see it is to ask what each approach actually saves during decoding, because the bottleneck in long-context decoding is mostly memory, not FLOPs.

With DeepSeek's sparse attention, the DSA approach in V3.2, you still keep the full KV cache. A lightweight indexer scores past tokens and picks a top-k subset for the main attention to attend to. That greatly reduces per-step attention compute, so long-context decoding gets cheaper and faster. But you still have to store every token's KV, and the indexer itself still touches all of them, though cheaply. So you save compute but not memory capacity. The upside is fidelity. Since nothing is thrown away, the model can in principle retrieve any exact token from far back. That's a big reason it can be converted from a dense model with continued training and stay close to full-attention quality.

The hybrid linear approach, like Kimi Linear with KDA layers interleaved with full MLA layers at roughly three to one, attacks memory directly. The linear layers compress the entire history into a fixed-size state, so for most layers the KV cache simply disappears and per-token decoding cost is constant. You save memory and compute together, which matters a lot when you're serving huge batches or very long agentic trajectories. The price is that a fixed-size state is lossy. Pure linear attention struggles with precise recall, like needle-in-a-haystack retrieval or copying. That's why you keep a few full-attention layers. They act as the exact-retrieval backbone, while the linear layers handle most of the local and compositional processing cheaply. And the delta rule matters here. A gated delta-rule update manages that finite memory much better than older linear attention, because it can overwrite and forget selectively instead of just accumulating.

So my summary is that sparse attention is "keep everything, read selectively," and hybrid linear is "compress most things, keep a few exact lookups." The first is safer on quality and easier to adopt, the second is more radical on efficiency. I don't think they're really competitors, though. They're orthogonal. You could easily imagine a hybrid model whose remaining full-attention layers are themselves sparse. That combination is where I'd expect things to converge for very long-context decoding.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says DeepSeek sparse attention still keeps the full KV cache while selecting only a top-k subset for attention.

r002.rationale: It describes KDA linear-attention layers interleaved with fewer full MLA layers, with the linear layers compressing history into a fixed-size state and eliminating most per-layer KV cache.

r003.rationale: It says the hybrid approach’s memory savings matter when serving huge batches.

r004.rationale: It explains that selecting a top-k subset reduces per-step attention computation, making long-context decoding cheaper and faster.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the cleanest way to frame it is that both teams are attacking the same problem, which is that the KV cache is the real bottleneck for long-context decoding, but they're attacking it from opposite ends.

Kimi's hybrid approach, with Kimi Linear, uses linear attention in most layers and keeps full attention in a minority of layers. The linear layers have constant-size state, so the cost per token is flat no matter how long the context is. The full attention layers still have a KV cache, but you've cut it by something like 75 percent. So at decode time, you've shrunk the memory and the bandwidth you have to touch per step. The trade-off is that linear attention is a compressed memory. You're squeezing the whole history into a fixed-size state, so by construction you lose some fine-grained retrieval ability. That's exactly why they keep a few full attention layers, to give the model a place to do precise lookups. The hybrid ratio is the knob you're tuning: more linear layers means cheaper decode, fewer means better retrieval.

DeepSeek's sparse attention goes the other way. They keep the entire KV cache, nothing is thrown away, but at each decode step they only attend to a selected subset of tokens. So the compute is sparse, but the memory footprint isn't reduced. You still pay to store all of it. What you save is the attention FLOPs and some of the bandwidth, because you're only reading the selected blocks. The upside is you preserve the ability to recall any token exactly. If the selection mechanism works, you get near-full-attention quality. The downside is that memory still grows linearly with context, so at a million tokens you're still carrying a huge cache, and the selector itself has to be good, because if it misses the right block you simply don't see it.

So I'd describe it like this. Linear attention is a lossy compression bet: you accept that you can't recall everything, and you make the common case extremely cheap. Sparse attention is a lossless storage, lossy compute bet: you keep everything, and you accept that you need a smart indexing mechanism to find it. Which one wins depends on what your workload looks like. For agentic settings where the model generates very long trajectories and you're mostly reasoning over recent context, hybrid linear is very attractive, because decode throughput dominates and memory per concurrent request matters a lot for serving. For tasks that need needle-in-a-haystack retrieval over long documents, sparse attention is safer, because it never discards the needle.

My personal view, from working on linear attention, is that these aren't really competing long-term. The natural end state is probably a hybrid of both: linear layers handling most of the sequence modeling, and the remaining attention layers being sparse rather than dense. The two ideas compose quite well. What Kimi and DeepSeek have shown is that each component works at scale on its own, which is the prerequisite for putting them together.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as two different ways to reduce the cost of accessing a long history during decoding.

With hybrid linear attention, some layers compress the history into a fixed-size state, while other layers retain conventional attention. That reduces the amount of KV-cache data you need to store and read at each decoding step. The trade-off is that compression can lose information: if you later need one precise detail from far back in the context, the compressed state may not preserve it well enough. The conventional attention layers help compensate for that.

Sparse attention keeps more of the history available as individual tokens, but reads only a selected subset for each query. That can be useful for precise retrieval, provided the selection mechanism finds the relevant tokens. You’re trading the cost of reading everything for the cost—and possible errors—of deciding what to read. Also, sparse reads don’t automatically mean a proportionally smaller KV cache.

So the central question is where you accept the bottleneck: compressing the past or selecting from it. For long-text decoding, I’d compare both at matched quality and on the same hardware, looking at latency, throughput, and cache memory. I’d especially test cases where a small detail early in the context becomes important much later. Without specifying the particular implementations, I wouldn’t say either approach is categorically better.

r001.rationale: It says sparse reads do not automatically mean a proportionally smaller KV cache, but does not state that DeepSeek still stores the full KV cache.

r002.rationale: It says some layers compress history into a fixed-size state, but does not identify them as RNN-like linear-attention layers or say they replace most attention layers.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect a smaller KV-cache footprint to larger decoding batch sizes.

r004.rationale: It says sparse attention reads a selected subset of history, but does not clearly state that sparse activation reduces per-token decoding computation.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame it as a trade-off between compressing the past and selectively revisiting it.

With hybrid linear attention, much of the history is represented in a fixed-size recurrent state. That can reduce KV-cache growth and memory traffic during decoding, which becomes especially attractive at very long context lengths. Keeping some full-attention layers helps preserve the ability to access individual tokens. The question is how much information the compressed state retains when the task requires precise recall.

Sparse attention keeps token-level representations but reads only a selected subset at each step. That gives it a more direct route to retrieving specific details from a long history, provided the selection mechanism finds the relevant tokens. You still have costs for storing the history, selecting tokens, and accessing potentially scattered memory.

So I wouldn’t judge the trade-off from attention complexity alone. I’d compare decoding latency and throughput at the same quality, context length, batch size, and hardware—and include cache memory and selection overhead. For summarizing broad context, compression may be very effective. For finding a small, exact detail buried far back, selective retrieval may have an advantage. The hybrid design is an attempt to capture both benefits; how well it succeeds is an empirical question.
